utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D5275 will receive number D534, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The evidence we've just discussed is now before the Court, Mr. Grekulovic, so we don't need to repeat what is in your statement or in the documents, but I want to ask you a few questions just to clarify and I won't be long.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have, please, on the screen Mr. Grekulovic's statement which is now D522.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go straight to paragraph 6, and the meeting that you had with Radovan Stojicic in late August of 1995. Before this meeting, were you aware of the agreement reached between the Republika Srpska government and the Serbian government about the provision of Serbian police forces to the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recall the words used by Badza concerning the object and purpose of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that he said that he needed some 400 police officers from the Special Police Units to extend assistance to the MUP of Republika Srpska in their policing works because they had a lot of refugees and a lot of security problems and that I had to go together with those men to the Republika Srpska to the locations that I previously mentioned in view of the fact that General Obrad Stevanovic was absent from the Republika Srpska, he had been re-assigned to carry out some tasks in Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recall what was said about refugees or the significance of refugees?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: It was said that the unit had to go there to help the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia in dealing with the security tasks pertaining to the work of the ministry. It was also said that those men had to see that Serbia did not turn their back on the population that had fled from the area of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the population of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Remember to take a little pause between sentences. I think you speak quite fast and what you are saying is being translated. What was said, if anything, at that meeting about the detention of deserters? How did that fit into your crime prevention activities?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: We were told that we would be helping the police of the Republika Srpska in bringing in deserters to the units because those men were armed and they were prone to disrupting public law and order, they were prone to crime. That's why they were supposed to report back to their units and another reason was to boost the efficiency of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you told anything at that meeting or did you learn anything subsequently about whether the Republika Srpska Bosnian Serbs were engaged in offensive or defensive operations or a mixture of the two at the time?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: I saw it only later when I entered the area. It was mostly a mixed operation but it was primarily a defensive operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Looking at paragraph 11 of your statement, there's a number of documents referred to. We don't need to turn to them at this point but within some of these documents there's mention of an operation called Kosovska Bosa. What was that operation? Mr. Grekulovic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: The name of the operation was Kosovski Bozur, the Kosovo Peony.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. What was that operation? What was its object and purpose?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: It was an operation that was permanent in nature. The objective was for the police of the Republika Srpska and the military police with the help of the police from Serbia to permanently work on bringing in deserters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Turning to paragraph 15, please, I want to just quickly try to clarify the structures that you found when you arrived, or rather, the structures that you fell within. You say at paragraph 15 that there was a joint staff which was set up in Banja Luka in order to defend the area. What was your men's relationship to that joint staff?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: My men assisted the regular police at the Security Services Centre in Doboj, Banja Luka and Prijedor. There were operative staffs there headed by chiefs of security centres. I was in the operative staff in Banja Luka together with Pecanac. The staff at the ministry level, I know that it was headed by Minister Kovac. I'm not aware of the entire composition of the staff, I don't know who all of its members were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So which was superior, the operative staff or the ministerial staff? Perhaps that's an obvious question, but just so we are clear.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: The ministerial staff was superior. The staff at the ministry level.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who -- so Kovac commanded the ministerial staff?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who commanded the staff at Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pecanac. He was the chief of the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's turn to paragraph 18, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, is there any way to clarify what joint staff it actually was. I mean, what was joint, what kind of units? Was it only MUP survey units or was it only the special anti-terrorist unit and -- it's unclear joint staff of what.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly, I'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Which kind of staff fell within -- fell underneath the ministerial staff? Let's deal with that first.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: At the ministry level there were all the three operative staffs at the level of the Security Services Centres. What I'm saying is that the three operative staffs were under the ministerial staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what did the operative staffs consist of? Were they all consisting of the same or were they different?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: Every operative staff had as their members chiefs of security centres. For example, the head of staff or the Chief of Staff was the chief of security. Members of the staff were the chief of crime prevention services at the security service centres. The chief of police, the chief of traffic police, the chief for logistics, the commander of the Special Police Unit, and the officer of the police unit from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's still for all the services mentioned, I do not know whether it's from Serbia or from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I was going to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Where did your men -- no, let me break this down a bit. Banja Luka, were the men who fell within the operative staff from Serbia or the Republika Srpska or a mixture of both?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: What I have just told you, all the officers were from the Republika Srpska. Only one officer, the officer that was of the unit that was in the area, that was deployed from the Republic of Serbia was actually from the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was the situation the same or different in the operative staff of Prijedor and the operative staff of Doboj?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were there men, the officers -- sorry, those, the rank and file of the police officers sent from Serbia divided amongst the three operative centres or what was the situation?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: They belonged to the 3 operative centres. That's how they were divided. And depending on the current operations of the police in each of the cities, their numerical strength would either be increased or decreased.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What do you mean by depending on the current operations of the police in each of the cities? What did it depend upon concretely?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about police operations: Increased traffic control, stepped up control at the check-points, the control of catering establishments, operations to arrest a larger number of people, and in more general terms all sorts of police operations that are normally carried out in urban areas, for example, raids as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Is that clear, Your Honour, or would you like me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if the witness wants to tell us that dependent on the operations there were more or less, then it's clear. However, if it has any other meaning, I would say it goes without saying that if there are more intensive operations that you need more people. To say that it gives a lot of information, no. If I have to understand the testimony like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't follow Your Honour's criticism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Depending on the current operations of the police in each of the cities their numerical strength would either be increased or decreased," which means if you have more operations, you have more men, if you had less. And then the witness explains that it's about police operation, increased traffic control, stepped up -- what he says is if police tasks were more intense, we needed more people. I mean, I would say that it doesn't give a lot of information apart from if you need more people, you have more people, if there are less needed, you have less.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What kind of police operations were you engaged in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's one of the things the witness said already, traffic police, et cetera, et cetera. What I'm interested in if it has any further meaning than if the more intensive operations, when did operations - and could you give us an example - more intensive.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, an intensive operation was, for example, Kosovski Bozur which was on-going and intensive in all places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what was the -- what was the operation about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was about bringing in deserters and military conscripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many people took that out of the 400?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was done in the territories of all the centres. Let me put it this way: Everybody was engaged depending on what they were doing, whether they were patrolling, whether they were doing searches or something else, so that people from all the centres were engaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an answer to my question. My question was how many of the 400 people that were sent there were involved in bringing in deserters and military conscripts? Or did all of them do it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everybody did it but the numbers varied from day-to-day. For example, on one day you could have 200 with 100 resting. On the following day you would have 150, which means that they all took part but not all at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And do I now have to understand that, for example, patrolling and check-points and searches, was that all focused on bringing in deserters or did you also perform police duties which were not directly related to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. There were also police tasks that weren't only about this, but every police task in -- starting from patrolling a territory, manning check-points, or doing traffic control, if you come across a deserter, you bring him in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's try to break that down a bit more, what you've just said. "Every police task in -- starting from patrolling a territory, manning check-points or doing traffic control, if you come across a deserter you bring him in." Did you have planning or briefing meetings whereby instructions were passed to the police officers who were operating in these three locations?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Each operative staff and each police station planned their activities in the context of carrying out these tasks and there was regular informing about that through the process of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And were the police officers given priorities? What were those priorities?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: One of the priorities was the implementation of measures that were part of the Bozur operation. That was one priority, but at any rate, when you carry out police tasks in the field, there are also other duties apart from that, namely controlling motor cars, their passengers, inspect catering facilities, and surveil public places.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And for you what was the object of -- what was the purpose of arresting the deserters? What were you achieving in your mind?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: What was achieved was that they were not leaving their units, thus reducing their combat readiness. And secondly, they weren't making trouble in towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What do you mean trouble in towns?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they didn't disturb public law and order, they didn't commit criminal offences, they didn't get drunk, they didn't engage in fights or do anything else that adversarially -- adversely affects security in any given place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. May I just take instructions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to look back now and assess what impact, if any, these 400 police officers had on the situation of law and order in the locations that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: From today's vantage point, I'm certain that there was an influence and that the police officers went about their duties professionally. By doing that, they made a significant contribution to the safety and security of citizens and that safety and security being at a satisfactory level.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, 5611, which is one of the so-called Mladic diaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I just want to ask you if you can clarify the situation in terms of refugees. Before we -- that comes to the screen, let me ask you during the time you were there what was the situation in terms of numbers of refugees and whether they increased or decreased during the time you were there, and whether you are able to say anything about numbers?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really couldn't comment on the numbers. There were many refugees. I only know that while we were going from Bijeljina to Banja Luka and Prijedor that we had a hard time moving on because of the long columns of refugees, but I don't know the exact number. I know that many stayed in the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me just clarify this, please. When you were going from Bijeljina to Banja Luka and Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. It was in early September. I don't know the exact date but soon after the fall of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who had a hard time moving because of the long columns of refugees?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: We did because we were moving in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You mean you were moving on one occasion or a number of occasions or what's the situation?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm referring about that one day when we entered and were travelling to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did the situation improve in terms of -- well, let me be specific. Did the number of refugees increase during the time you were there or increase -- decrease or increase?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in Banja Luka it increased because after that the citizens of Sanski Most and Mrkonjic Grad also left their towns and came to Banja Luka so that the total numbers increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And by the time you left, are you able to say anything about the situation then?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: You mean when I returned to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, by the time you and your men left to return to Serbia, what was the situation with refugees as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: There were really very many refugees. A large number. The situation had calmed down because the Dayton Accord was already signed, but many refugees stayed in the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you say many refugees, are we talking tens, hundreds, thousands? What are we talking?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but I think it must have been thousands. We are talking about thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've got nothing further for you, Mr. Witness. Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Before I give the Simatovic Defence an opportunity, when you are talking about refugees, are you talking about Serbs seeking refuge in Republika Srpska, is that what you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And at what time in -- what point in time do you put the Dayton Agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when the agreement was signed there had already been a cease-fire, a truce. There were no more combat activities and the situation was far better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when you are referring to the Dayton Agreement, you are referring to the period immediately prior to that which had already its effect on hostilities; is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all activities preceded the Dayton Accord. The refugees from Sanski Most and Mrkonjic Grad had arrived before the Dayton Accord. Once the latter was signed, there were no more combat activities and no more new refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, is it you or will it be Mr. Bakrac who cross-examines the witness? It's you, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Grekulovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Bakrac is counsel for Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Grekulovic.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I only have a few questions for you. Here is my first question: How long did you stay in Banja Luka in 1995, or in Bosnia in general?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: I think around 47 days, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: During those 47 days in that territory, did you ever see Franko Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, the first two questions, the answers do already appear in the statement, isn't it? 47 is 46 to 47, never seen Mr. Simatovic is in the statement. Please proceed, but preferably in addition to what we have already read. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I wanted to lay a foundation for the following question: Namely, did you hear from anybody in the field that Franko Simatovic was present in that territory?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. In paragraph 18 you mention Mr. Dragan Filipovic, a member of the State Security Service of the Republic of Serbia. During the proofing with today's date, you said that Mr. Filipovic was some sort of liaison between the MUP forces that had been sent there to control crime and the headquarters of the Serbian MUP in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say a sort of liaison, does that mean that Mr. Dragan Filipovic had -- was in radio communication with cryptographic protection in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to object. I don't believe Mr. Bakrac is accurately quoting the proofing note that we made today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please make a literal quote, Mr. Bakrac. If there's any discussion about the accuracy of a quote, make it a literal quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, if I understand correctly, you stated that Filipovic worked with another DB operative, one Dujovic and that they were some sort of liaison between the MUP of Serbia and the forces that had been deployed to assist in crime enforcement in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The quote that I have is that Filipovic also worked with another DB operative Dujovic, who was some kind of liaison between the Serbian MUP police forces sent to help control crime in Belgrade. The modification is on who Dujovic is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I asked you to quote literally, is Mr. Weber more literally quoting than you were, because there seems to be a difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree that Mr. Weber quoted correctly in English, but let me first ask the witness if he gave his proofing statement in English or in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you utter that statement in English or in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: In Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I never received the Serbian version. This proofing note and the witness's statement I understand them this way, but we can now clarify it with the witness. Did he mean that both Filipovic and Dujovic were some sort of liaison or maybe only Filipovic or again only Dujovic. Am I allowed to put this question to the witness, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ... Let me -- first, totally different question. Who took the proofing statement? Is that, was it you, was it --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It was me, with Ms. Dobrota.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the statement was translated to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And this what we see in an e-mail exchange on which the Chamber was copied, and I read it later so that it will be in the -- on the record, was it just as simple as in this one line or was there any further discussion on the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There was further discussion on the matter and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently the issue here is, and I'm -- witness, do you understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you take -- could you take off your earphones for a second. What apparently seems to be the difference between the two versions is that as you read it in English here, the DB operative Dujovic is described as some kind of a liaison between the Serbian MUP police forces sent to help control crime and Belgrade, whereas in the questioning of Mr. Bakrac apparently some attention is paid to or at least is suggested that not only Mr. Dujovic but Mr. Filipovic had a similar function. Is that well understood, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour, because the sentence started "that Filipovic also worked with another DB operative" and then explanation who, "who was some kind of liaison," et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And for me it's really unclear, my understanding is that the both of them working as liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That does not follow logically from the language used.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Then it's my fault entirely, I can tell you what the witness told me, the witness told me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First, Mr. Weber is on his feet as well, it's a bit of --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I was on first, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I know that, I know that. I asked you something, isn't it? What I wanted to ask Mr. Weber is whether he objects to you now giving a kind of -- because that's apart from hearsay, of course, we are entering at this moment we are trying to find out to what extent what we read here what it means apart from asking the witness, Mr. Jordash is offering at this moment to explain because I asked him whether it was just this one line or whether there was more, that he explains to us how he understood the conversation. Is there any objection to proceeding in this way, Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. Any relevant information should have been included in the proofing note with respect to who this individual Dujovic is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But apparently the proofing he note is here unclear and to say that it should have been in there is nice but doesn't resolve the problem, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Correct. The Prosecution is receiving late notice. The Stanisic Defence decided not to lead this evidence as part of their examination. It is now coming up with the co-accused examination and the Stanisic Defence wishes to add information into the proofing note which is unknown to the Prosecution. What we would suggest is the following: Is that whatever the Stanisic Defence has as further information in relation to this conversation or this proofing, that in relation to this matter, that they write it down, that they send us a proofing note, we'll look at it and if the Simatovic Defence, after we look at it, wants to conduct further examination, then both parties are on notice of what this information is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will proceed as follows: We'll allow Mr. Jordash so tell the Chamber how he understood the conversation and to what extent it is well or less well reflected in the one-liner, then we'll after that ask the witness to put his earphones on and finally I may ask some questions in relation to what is here and then the parties can put further questions to the witness. Mr. Jordash, before I invite you to do what you intended to do already, has the witness ever read this line?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Was it your impression that he had any understanding of the English language?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not at all. Then please tell us how you understood the conversation which led you to write down these two lines, or which led the Stanisic Defence to write down these two lines, because I cannot I am not allowed to take you as the author without further information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The witness's response came in relation to questions I was asking him about Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what he meant when he said that Filipovic had co-ordinated the activities of the forces of the MUP of Serbia. The witness said in fact that what Filipovic was doing was acting as some form of liaison and when the witness needed some assistance, he would speak to Filipovic or if he needed to consult, he would speak to Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Consult whom or assist in what? If that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Assist in -- if, for example, the Serbian MUP police officers needed further supplies such as food or cigarettes, they would speak to Filipovic, and if they had queries about the use of those forces in crime prevention, they would also speak to Filipovic, and he in that role played a liaison role with Belgrade. And then the witness mentioned Dujovic and said that Dujovic was a subordinate of Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That was the sum total of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put on your earphones again. Yes, can you hear me again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what Mr. Dujovic's task was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His task was, in my view, to be a link between myself and Mr. Filipovic. To be more precise, he acted as a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Liaising between you and Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He was with me all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And why would he liaise with Mr. Filipovic, on what kind of matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He mostly made sure that the units carried out the tasks for which they were deployed in the first place. He also made sure that all the tasks were being carried out in a professional manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are talking about he. My question he was why Mr. Dujovic would liaise with Mr. Filipovic, so "he" is unclear and could refer to Mr. Dujovic or Mr. Filipovic. Are you telling us that it was Mr. Dujovic who was mostly made sure that the units carried out the tasks for which they were deployed? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The two of us did that, but he was that link between me and Mr. Filipovic because I didn't have permanent contacts with Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was he liaising about? Was it about the weather forecast? Was it about uniforms? Was it about operational matters? Was it about logistical matters? What kind of matters -- on what kind of matters he liaised between you and Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mostly this was about logistics. Whatever I needed from Belgrade went through Mr. Dujovic and I believe that it also went through Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did Mr. Dujovic then directly relay -- liaise between you and Belgrade or was the next step left to Mr. Filipovic? Who would be in touch with Belgrade, Mr. Dujovic or Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't be able to tell you who communicated with Belgrade. However, if I needed anything, I would communicate with Mr. Dujovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you do not know who finally got in touch with Belgrade, whether that was Mr. Dujovic, himself, or whether it was Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. I was in no position to know that. I only know that I contacted him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless he would have told you Belgrade told me A or B or Belgrade will send this and that, so that you were in no position to know that depends on what he told you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. And that concerns the logistics part because I didn't have anything to do with Belgrade. I couldn't communicate with Belgrade because all the lines were down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although it's not an answer to my question, but could you please tell us logistics about what? Was that about vehicles? Was that about food? Was that about ammunition? What kind of logistics are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, I asked them to provide food because there was not enough food for my men, and I also asked for cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what about ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not need ammunition. We were not involved in any combat. We had our own personal weapons and the ammunition that we brought with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We used those vehicles that we brought with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No need for spare parts or any other parts needed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no need for that. I relied on the MUP of the Republika Srpska for fuel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now anything else apart from food and cigarettes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not request anything. The only thing that I did not have enough of was food and cigarettes. I had everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I'm looking at the clock. I promised five minutes to Mr. Jordash. First of all, would you have further questions on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one with your leave and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Strictly leave it to that, leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Grekulovic, did you hear from Mr. Dujovic perhaps since you said that you didn't have any direct communication lines with Belgrade, did you hear from Mr. Dujovic if Mr. Filipovic has a protected line with Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN GREKULOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know how they communicated -- communicated with Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, that was my one question. And tomorrow I will need another 15 minutes with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just about to ask you that. Another 15 minutes tomorrow. Mr. Grekulovic, we have to conclude for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom, Courtroom II, and I hereby instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether that is testimony that you gave already today or whether that's testimony still to be given tomorrow or the day after tomorrow. Is that clear to you? So not to speak or not to communicate in any other way about your testimony. Then you may follow the usher and we'd like to see you back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, do you want to address us in open session or private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Open, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours will probably have seen the medical report from today, the 25th of November, 2011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't seen it yet, to be quite honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There's nothing in there that I think hasn't been in there before, but there is at paragraph 7 reference to a telephone conference of the 3rd of November, 2011, between Dr. Van Geenan at the Bronovo hospital and two foreign doctors, Dr. Chan and Dr. Tarabar and their decision that Mr. Stanisic's medication had to be changed. Your Honour will see in that paragraph that the first two, [indiscernible] of that medicine have to be taken under medical supervision of Dr. Van Geenan at the Bronovo hospital or the JMC. It's still not clear when this will take place. By changing the medication, the complaints will probably diminish and the physical condition will improve. I wanted to raise the issue of the delay in giving Mr. Stanisic that treatment. It's been some time. Apparently there is a delay concerning biopsy reports from a clinic in Leiden, nonetheless we are not clear as to why there's this long delay, and it's of real concern to Mr. Stanisic obviously. It's of real concern to this Stanisic Defence. It is almost impossible -- it feels almost impossible to try to obtain information beyond these quite sparse reports that we receive on a weekly basis, which frankly do not assist in helping Mr. Stanisic and certainly don't assist me in trying to speak to Mr. Stanisic about the current problem or problems. At the same time, we have at paragraph 4, sorry, paragraph 14, the following: "The above taken in consideration, I cannot explain Mr. Stanisic's claim that he is more tired than before and is not able to visit court in the present frequency." While it seems in my respectful submission that there might well be a good explanation for that, that he has been recommended treatment on the 3rd of November and he still has yet to have it, and that treatment, according to the doctor, would diminish or would probably diminish his physical ailment. There's a very good reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Maybe, maybe not, I mean, I'm not a doctor, but what I do understand is you have two specific questions, why did it take so long. That's the first one. And the second is, could this delay have caused what Mr. Stanisic tells us that he is unable to visit court at the present frequency, could any link be between the two, is that -- that's how I understood your --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. On top of that, Your Honour, I've been instructed by Mr. Stanisic to assist him in trying to obtain information from his treating doctors. I have approached the commander of the UNDU and I've been told that somehow sitting down with Mr. Stanisic's treating doctor would interfere with the client/patient relationship. I'm seeking clarification from OLAD as to why that would be and why Mr. Stanisic hasn't got the right to ask somebody to assist him with obtaining information about his own medical condition, especially in light of the fact that his English is not by any stretch --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a third matter, why are you not allowed to receive, together with Mr. Stanisic, the information he is seeking and you have no access to?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. And it's an on-going problem. In terms of obtaining information. I really feel as though I have to face Mr. Stanisic every day and say I'm not sure how to help you because I just cannot get the information that I need. Neither can he, more importantly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not giving you any answer to any of the questions what explanations could be or not, but the Chamber will inquire into the matter and I leave it to that and usually if we inquire into something, then we do it rather intensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can count on the Chamber in that respect. Another matter is the, that first medication has been given now or is still to be given soon, has any appointment been made for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: As far as we know no appointment has been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see Mr. Stanisic is nodding no, so that appointment still has to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's when paragraph number 7 also confirms is not clear when this will take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll pay proper attention to the concerns you have expressed, Mr. Jordash, were these the three major matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll adjourn and we resume tomorrow, the -- let me see, Tuesday, the 29th of November, 2011, in this same Courtroom II at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 29th day of November, 2011 at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
